url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

When you’re dealing with “currency valuations over time” you’re essentially looking at a **time‑series** problem. Below are the most common ways to represent such data, along with their trade‑offs so you can pick the one that fits your workload. | Approach | Typical representation | Pros | Cons | |----------|------------------------|------|------| | **Python `dict` / `OrderedDict`** | `{timestamp: value}` (or `OrderedDict` if order matters) | • Very lightweight
• Fast lookups by exact key | • No built‑in range queries
• Requires manual sorting if you need chronological order | | **List of tuples / list of objects** | `[(ts1, val1), (ts2, val2), …]` | • Simple, no external libs
• Easy to serialize to JSON/CSV | • Linear search for arbitrary timestamps
• Range queries require scanning | | **Pandas `Series` / `DataFrame`** | `pd.Series(data, index=pd.DatetimeIndex([...]))` | • Built‑in resampling, rolling windows, interpolation
• Vectorised arithmetic
• Handles missing data gracefully | • Memory overhead (especially for very long series)
• Requires installing pandas | | **SQLite + `datetime` column** | Table `(timestamp TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value REAL)` | • Persistent storage
• SQL range queries (`WHERE timestamp BETWEEN ? AND ?`)
• Indexes improve lookup speed | • Overhead of SQL parsing
• Not ideal for high‑frequency streaming writes | | **Time‑series DB (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus)** | Native TS engine | • Optimised for write‑heavy workloads
• Built‑in downsampling & retention policies
• Powerful query languages (Flux, SQL extensions) | • Extra infrastructure
• Learning curve for query language | | **Redis Sorted Set** | `ZADD key ts score` | • Extremely fast inserts & range queries
• Keeps data in memory (fast access) | • Limited persistence (unless configured)
• Need to manage eviction policy | ### When to choose each | Scenario | Recommended structure | |----------|-----------------------| | You’re prototyping or have a small dataset (< 10⁶ points) | Pandas `Series` (easiest to work with) | | You need persistent storage but don’t want a full DBMS | SQLite (simple, zero‑config) | | You’ll ingest millions of updates per second and need real‑time analytics | InfluxDB / TimescaleDB | | You already run Redis for caching and want quick in‑memory access | Redis Sorted Set | | You need to join this series with other tabular data frequently | Pandas DataFrame (or a relational DB) | --- #### Quick Python example with Pandas ```python import pandas as pd from datetime import datetime # Sample data data = { '2024-01-01T00:00:00': 1.12, '2024-01-02T00:00:00': 1.15, '2024-01-03T00:00:00': 1.13, } # Create a Series indexed by DatetimeIndex ts = pd.Series(data=data) ts.index = pd.to_datetime(ts.index) print(ts) # 2024-01-01 00:00:00 1.12 # 2024-01-02 00:00:00 1.15 # 2024-01-03 00:00:00 1.13 # dtype: float64 # Resample to weekly average weekly_avg = ts.resample('W').mean() print(weekly_avg) ``` If you’re working in another language (JavaScript, Java, C#, etc.), let me know and I can show analogous patterns (e.g., `Map` in JS, `TreeMap` in Java, or using libraries like Apache Commons Math). Feel free to tell me more about: * Your typical data volume (points per day, total days). * How you plan to query it (point lookups, range scans, aggregations). * Whether you need persistence or just in‑memory processing. That way I can narrow down the recommendation even further!
